chunks: "I draw a vertical line for the base region, with the base lead coming in horizontally from the left.
On the right side of that bar I draw two slanted lines, one going up to the collector and one going down to the emitter. The emitter line gets an arrowhead.
For an NPN, the arrow points away from the base, out of the transistor, toward the emitter terminal. A PNP is the mirror image where the arrow points into the base.
The way I remember it is that the arrow is the base-emitter diode: it points from P to N, which is the direction conventional current flows when that junction conducts.
In an NPN the base is P and the emitter is N, so the arrow goes from base to emitter, outward. Another mnemonic is NPN, 'Not Pointing iN'.

Then I'd label the terminals B, C and E, and add the currents: for an NPN, collector current flows into the collector, base current flows into the base, and both leave through the emitter, so I E equals I C plus I B .
Typically the collector goes up to the load and supply and the emitter goes down toward ground."
